subject: CedarLogic private deploy — data-plane ingress transport selection

Subject: CedarLogic private deploy - data-plane ingress options

Thanks Karthik / Ben —

We're kicking off work to run Redwood Private inside our VPCs and on our co-lo. NetOps asked for a short decision guidance: we need to pick an ingress model for the data-plane (the inference request path) — options on the table are VPC peering, interface endpoints/PrivateLink, or a site-to-site VPN (we also have a Direct Connect circuit but bandwidth is currently constrained).

Key constraints:
- Production SLA: 99.95%
- Typical request size: synchronous text generation, P50 latency target ~80ms, p99 < 500ms
- Traffic profile: ~120 qps steady, spiky bursts to 700 qps for short periods
- Security: mutually authenticated TLS required, and we need tenant-level audit logs into our SIEM
- IP addressing: limited private CIDR space (10.x), prefer to avoid large routing table explosion

I've attached our network diagram and a small traffic sample. Can you give pros/cons + a recommended path and a short checklist for NetOps? Ideally by Monday.

Thanks,
Alex
Alex Murphy
Head of Platform, CedarLogic

Hi Alex —

Thanks for the context and diagrams. High level thoughts up front: there is no one-size-fits-all — choice depends on region alignment, cross-account trust model, CIDR availability and expected throughput. Quick summary here, followed by a recommended hybrid approach.

Short pros/cons (TL;DR):
- VPC peering: low-latency, good for same-cloud & same-region, but no transitive routing (won't work across multiple cloud accounts/regions without extra peering), and you expose routes between networks which increases blast radius. Requires free CIDR space and route-table entries.
- Interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink / interface ENIs): strong isolation (Redwood's service appears as an endpoint service), minimal route-table churn, easier to enforce IAM/policies and audit. There is an ENI per AZ which can increase IP use; per-connection throughput is generally good but has more hops and costs per hour and per GB. Best when you want a narrow ingress surface and strong non-transitive isolation.
- Site-to-site VPN: flexible (on-premises to cloud), simple to set up as a fallback, but less predictable latency and throughput — spikes can saturate the tunnel, and it relies on on-prem edge hardware. For production throughput at your scale we'd typically recommend a managed VPN + Direct Connect as a stable path.

Recommended initial pattern: Prefer interface endpoints (PrivateLink) when you want an isolated service endpoint (strong security posture, easier auditing). Use VPC peering if CedarLogic prefers flat IP-level connectivity in the same account/region and can allocate CIDR space safely. Use S2S VPN only as a fallback / for on-prem sites where you can't place ENIs or peering (or until Direct Connect is available).

I'll put together a short checklist and an annotated decision matrix. Can you confirm whether the workload will be in the same AWS account/region as the Redwood host VPC or if we need cross-account access? Also whether logs must traverse your VPC to reach your SIEM or if Redwoods' audit log export to your S3 is acceptable?

-karthik

Adding a few technical tradeoffs and operational notes from infra: 

1) Latency & throughput
- Peering is typically lowest latency (L2/L3 reachability inside the cloud), but you pay egress/ingress data transfer per cloud's pricing model. For spikes of ~700 qps we want to ensure we have node-level capacity and consider connection pooling on the client side.
- PrivateLink has an extra hop through the ENI and NLB (if we front with an NLB in the service owner account) but we can tune connections and keep latencies in-budget for most text gen use-cases.

2) IP management and route table blow-up
- With large enterprise customers we often see route table explosion when peering many VPCs — that becomes an ops burden. PrivateLink scales better for many customers because it avoids needing per-customer routes.

3) Security boundaries and least privilege
- PrivateLink allows us to present an explicit service endpoint and avoid opening wide routes. It also plays more nicely with AWS PrivateLink policy controls.

4) Multi-region and DR
- If you need active-active across regions, peering is more complex (multiple peerings) whereas PrivateLink can be set up per region with region-aware failover. For on-prem DR you will likely want Direct Connect + transit options rather than relying solely on VPN.

Operational ask: can CedarLogic provide a short runbook of how your client side will pool connections and a list of AZs you will test from? That will let us size the ENI/NLB backend appropriately.

-Ben

Thanks — some clarifications from NetOps:
- Workloads will be in our primary AWS account (us-west-2). We will also have an on-prem co-lo site in the same metro that will need access; co-lo traffic should be routed via our VPCs.
- We cannot expand CIDR assignments right now (we're stuck on a /16 split across teams).
- Audit logs must arrive in our SIEM (Splunk) in near-real time; pulling logs from S3 is an option but NetOps prefers a push model (they run a collector inside the VPC).
- Mutual TLS is required and CedarLogic prefers connection pinning to a client cert issued by our CA.

Given the limited CIDR availability, and the desire to avoid many route entries, PrivateLink sounds attractive — but we worry about high-throughput bursts and per-GB costs and whether the ENI limits will be a blocker. What's your recommended plan for a high-traffic pilot?

-Alex

Alex —

Based on NetOps constraints (single account, no CIDR expansion, collector in-VPC, mutual TLS desire) here's an operational recommendation that balances performance and manageability. I've attached a one-page recommendation and a short checklist.

Final recommendation (Pilot -> Production):
1) Pilot: Use PrivateLink (interface endpoints) per region with an NLB-backed service in Redwood's account. Reasons: avoids adding peering routes, gives the narrowest ingress surface for audit and IAM controls, and integrates cleanly with your in-VPC Splunk collector. For burst handling we will provision extra backend capacity and pre-warm connections; Redwood will provide a connection pooling guide for the client side.

2) Scale / Production: If pilot shows steady high-throughput with p99 latency < 400ms, continue PrivateLink. If you see sustained sustained high-throughput (>= 1Gbps sustained) and want lower per-GB costs / fewer per-request charges, evaluate a transition to VPC peering + internal NLB with strict security ACLs — but that requires CIDR work and broader route exposure.

3) On-prem collector: route co-lo traffic through your VPC (transit via existing Direct Connect when available). In the interim, set up a redundant S2S VPN from co-lo to the VPC for failover; do not send production traffic over the VPN unless you validate bandwidth headroom.

Checklist (high level):
- Network: allocate ENI capacity and ensure at least one spare IP per AZ for the endpoint.
- Auth: implement mTLS with your CA; Redwood will support client cert pinning.
- Logging: configure Redwood to stream audit logs to an S3 bucket and set up a near-real-time Kinesis/Firehose forwarder that your Splunk collector can read from inside the VPC. (If push-only is required, we can run a lightweight forwarder in your VPC via a short-term support agreement.)
- Tests: run a pilot with synthetic traffic (spike tests to 700 qps and soak at 200 qps for 24h). Capture p50/p95/p99 and tail jitter.
- Rollback plan: if latency or costs exceed thresholds, we will pause new customers on PrivateLink and evaluate peering.

Attachments: ingress-recommendation-v1.pdf (detailed matrix), latency-benchmarks.xlsx (expected numbers from our staging region).

Proposed owners & next steps:
- CedarLogic NetOps: deploy ENI/security groups + run pilot traffic (owner: Alex).
- Redwood Infra: pre-provision backend capacity and provide connection pooling guide + test harness (owner: Ben).
- Integration: Karthik to coordinate audit-log forwarding and cert exchange.

If that works I can block an hour this week to walk NetOps through the pilot runbook.

-karthik
